sections.h2: Where is Cambridge, Massachusetts, and how is it organized?
sections.html:
Cambridge is a city in Middlesex County directly across the Charles River from Boston. It has 7.1 square miles of area, 6.4 of them land, and the 2020 census counted 118,403 residents, which made it the fourth-largest city in the state after Boston, Worcester and Springfield.

Somerville lies to the north, Arlington to the northwest, and Belmont and Watertown to the west. The city runs a council-manager government, and its ZIP codes run from 02138 to 02142.

Cambridge calls itself a city of squares, because most commercial districts sit at major street intersections that act as neighborhood centers. That shapes how people describe where a house is.

sections.h2: What are Cambridge's squares and neighborhoods?
sections.html:
Each square anchors a part of the city, and buyers often ask which one a house is closest to. Wikipedia describes these centers.

  • Kendall Square, at Broadway, Main Street and Third Street, is the biotech and technology center near MIT and the Kendall/MIT Red Line station.
  • Central Square, at Massachusetts Avenue, Prospect Street and Western Avenue, has a Red Line stop and a mix of restaurants.
  • Harvard Square, at Massachusetts Avenue, Brattle Street and JFK Street, has the Harvard Red Line station and Cambridge Common nearby.
  • Porter Square has both a Red Line stop and a Fitchburg Line commuter rail stop.
  • Inman Square sits at Cambridge and Hampshire Streets, and Lechmere Square is next to CambridgeSide.

Neighborhoods such as Cambridgeport, Baldwin (formerly Agassiz, renamed in 2021) and Mid-Cambridge round out the map. A listing that names the square it is closest to gives a buyer an instant sense of place.

sections.h2: What is the history behind Cambridge?
sections.html:
Cambridge was settled in 1630, was first called Newtowne, and was renamed Cambridge in May 1638 after the English university town. Harvard College was founded here in 1636, and the city was incorporated in 1846.

George Washington took command of the Continental Army on Cambridge Common in July 1775, so the Common is called the birthplace of the Army. Brattle Street was once nicknamed Tory Row because Loyalist families lived there in mansions.

Manufacturing was important in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and areas such as Kendall Square and East Cambridge were once centers of manufacturing before turning to biotech, labs and offices. Older buildings from each era remain across the city.

Universities and biotechnology firms dominate. Wikipedia lists the ten largest employers as of 2024.

sections.h2: How do you get around Cambridge?
sections.html:
The MBTA Red Line is the spine of the city, with stops at Kendall/MIT, Central, Harvard and Porter squares. Porter Square also has a commuter rail stop on the Fitchburg Line.

Harvard Square is still a major bus terminal. Before the West Boston Bridge opened in 1792, crossing from Cambridge to Boston meant an eight-mile trip by road around the Boston Neck, and bridges over the Charles River now tie the two cities together.

If your house is a short walk from a Red Line stop, put that in the description.

sections.h2: How does Cambridge assess property and bill taxes?
sections.html:
The Assessing Department values property at what Massachusetts calls full and fair cash value, which is 100 percent of fair market value. It uses cost, income and market approaches and submits values to the state Department of Revenue for certification before bills are issued.

The office is at 795 Massachusetts Avenue, Ground Floor, and the phone is 617-349-4343. For municipal lien certificates and online payments, the Finance Department is at 617-349-4220. Municipal lien certificates matter when you sell, since they show what is owed on the property.

The city's Fiscal Year 2027 abatement period ran from October 19 to November 18, 2026, with online help sessions through November 12. Residential exemption and personal exemption applications for FY27 are due April 1, 2027. The city says that owner-occupants can reduce their bill through the residential exemption. See the Assessing page for the current schedule.

sections.h2: What else shapes a Cambridge house sale?
sections.html:
The city's finances and its water system both show up in a sale. Cambridge held AAA ratings from Moody's, S&P and Fitch for 22 consecutive years as of 2021, and Wikipedia says its large commercial tax base has helped keep residential taxes fairly low. Its budget is the second largest in the state even though it is fourth in population.

Cambridge also runs its own municipal water system, including the Payson Park Reservoir in Belmont and the Hobbs Brook and Stony Brook watersheds in neighboring towns. The Assessing page warns that a first-half FY27 tax bill can carry a Water and Sewer Lien, so check your bill and call the Finance Department if one appears before you list or sign a contract.

The universities add another layer. MIT has a 168-acre campus here, and Harvard was founded in the city in 1636. Wikipedia also places Lesley University's University Hall and Porter campus at Porter Square,.

sections.h2: Why can Cambridge sales be slow or complicated?
sections.html:
Cambridge houses often come with specific complications: older construction, multi-unit buildings, tenants and historic districts.

  • Tenants in a two- or three-family can affect showings and the closing date.
  • Estate sales take time because of probate.
  • Condominium sales require documents from the association.
  • Older houses can need work before a buyer's lender will move forward.

These are general sale issues, not Cambridge rules. If any apply to you, a direct cash sale is one way to avoid showings and repairs.

sections.h2: What do you need to sell a house in Cambridge?
sections.html:
Massachusetts charges a deed excise tax of $2.00 for each $500 of price or fraction of $500 under MGL c. 64D, s. 1, and the registry of deeds collects it when the deed is recorded. The Department of Fire Services also requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the sale rules.

Book that inspection when you have a closing date, because the department charges a fee. Alarms older than ten years or past their expiration must be replaced with ten-year sealed photoelectric alarms with a hush feature.

Gather your deed, the latest tax bill, any lien information and permit records. Cash Home Buyers can review a Cambridge house as it stands and give you a written number to compare with a listing.

faqs.q: What county is Cambridge, MA in?
faqs.a: Cambridge is in Middlesex County, directly across the Charles River from Boston.
The 2020 census counted 118,403 residents, which made Cambridge the fourth-largest city in Massachusetts.

faqs.q: Who are the biggest employers in Cambridge?
faqs.a: Harvard University is first with 13,630 employees as of 2024, followed by MIT with 9,301 and the Cambridge Innovation Center with 5,011.

faqs.q: When is the residential exemption deadline in Cambridge?
faqs.a: For fiscal year 2027, the city lists April 1, 2027 as the due date for residential and personal exemption applications.

faqs.q: How do I contact the Cambridge Assessing Department?
faqs.a: Call 617-349-4343 or visit 795 Massachusetts Avenue, Ground Floor. For lien certificates, call the Finance Department at 617-349-4220.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke detector certificate to sell in Cambridge?
faqs.a: Yes. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department for a home sale or transfer.
